title: If not higher (Peretz, 1900)
hookLine: a skeptic follows the rebbe of Nemirov at dawn and finds him chopping wood for a sick widow

lines: THE REBBE IS MISSING AT DAWN.
A SKEPTIC DECIDES TO FIND OUT.
cards: In the town of Nemirov, the rumor was about the rebbe. Every morning in the days before the High Holy Days, when the congregation gathered before dawn to say the penitential prayers, the rebbe was missing. Where was he?

His followers had an answer: he goes up to heaven, of course, to plead for us. Then a visitor from Lithuania arrived, a sharp, skeptical scholar who didn't believe a word of it. And he decided to find out.

teach.b: I. L. Peretz wrote this story in Yiddish, and published it in 1900.
The skeptic, called the Litvak, hides under the rebbe's bed overnight. Before dawn, the rebbe gets up, and he doesn't put on his holy clothes.
He puts on peasant clothes, boots and a big belt, and takes an axe and a rope. The Litvak follows him, shivering, out of town and into the woods.
The rebbe chops down a small tree, splits it into logs, ties a bundle and carries it to a broken-down hut.
Inside lies a poor, sick widow. The rebbe speaks like a peasant: I've got wood to sell, cheap. She says: I can't pay.
He says: I'll trust you. You have a great and mighty God, and you don't trust Him for a few pennies?
Then he kneels and lays the wood in her stove, and with each log he murmurs a line of the dawn prayers. He lights the fire, and leaves. The Litvak stays in Nemirov and becomes the rebbe's disciple.
And from then on, when anyone says that at dawn the rebbe goes up to heaven, the Litvak doesn't laugh.
He just adds, quietly: if not higher. Helping someone in secret, without credit, without even letting her know who you are, is placed above the heavens.
And it closes a week of stories: the narrow bridge, the lost princess, the turkey prince, where is God, the crying baby, what hurts, and if not higher.

how: Peretz's story is read in Jewish schools and often retold around the High Holy Days; it echoes the Jewish ideal of giving in secret, so that the one who receives isn't shamed.

o: a Hasidic title for a rebbe's attendant
a woodcutter who sells logs to poor widows
a Jew from Lithuania, here the skeptic in the story

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.

s: the story is an old Hasidic legend written down centuries ago
it's a Yiddish short story by I. L. Peretz, published in 1900.
the rebbe tells the widow who he is
he speaks as a peasant and leaves without credit.
with each log, the rebbe says part of the dawn prayers
the chore and the prayer happen at the same time.

games.q: you're the Litvak. you've seen the rebbe chop wood for a widow in secret. now the Hasidim say he goes up to heaven. what do you say?
o: that's nonsense. I saw him in the woods.
games.why: the skeptic becomes a disciple, and quietly adds: if not higher. secret kindness outranks the rumor of heaven.

practice: Think of one small, useful thing you could do for someone who'd never know it was you: pay for something quietly, fix what's broken, leave a kind note unsigned, refill what everyone forgets.
Picture doing it and walking away without a word, notice how much of you wants credit, and let that part rest. If you pray, offer it as a prayer.

wordCard.voice: Litvak, the skeptical scholar from Lithuania who followed the rebbe of Nemirov at dawn. He saw him chop wood for a widow in secret, and said: if not higher.

orig.note: Yiddish: if not even higher, the title of Peretz's 1900 story.

carryVoice: Your line: kindness with no credit. The widow never knew who brought the wood. A week of stories, done.
